title: 'Shots fired, I need assistance now!' SIU report details chaotic shooting that left OPP officer and 60-year-old man dead on Manitoulin Island
subtitle: Investigators uncovered a trove of weapons and dangerous materials on the property where Const. Marc Hovingh was killed, including "dozens of improvised explosives and incendiary materials on the property, and numerous firearms inside the trailer."
article: Ontario's police watchdog has detailed the harrowing moments before the on-duty death of OPP Const. Marc Hovingh on Manitoulin Island, a November 2020 shootout that also killed the 60-year-old man who fired on the officer.

The Special Investigations Unit (SIU) was called in to investigate the death of Gary Brohman, who was shot dead inside his trailer in an exchange of gunfire with Hovingh on Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron.

According to the SIU, Brohman fired three times with his pump-action shotgun at Hovingh after police tried to arrest him for mischief. "Caught by surprise," Hovingh, a 28-year OPP veteran, fired back seven times - a response that was "squarely" justified as self-defence, according to a detailed report released by SIU director Joseph Martino on Friday.
"In the circumstances, it would appear that the officer had only split seconds to react, and may have even been wounded, by the time he drew his gun and started to fire back," Martino wrote.
Martino's report reveals the circumstances leading up to Hovingh's shooting, a rare on-duty death that prompted an outpouring of grief in Manitoulin Island and across the province.

In the aftermath of the shooting, investigators uncovered a trove of weapons and dangerous materials on the property where Brohman had "unlawfully" set up his trailer, including "dozens of improvised explosives and incendiary materials on the property, and numerous firearms inside the trailer," according to the report.
A photo provided by the Special Investigations Unit shows the trailer "unlawfully" set up by Gary Brohman, who was killed in a shoot-out with OPP Const. Marc Hovingh in November 2020.

The SIU said the incident began with the discovery, by an unnamed male civilian witness, that Brohman had bulldozed a road and set up a trailer on his property, located northeast of Gore Bay, about two hours southwest of Sudbury. When the property owner told Brohman he had to leave, he refused, the report said.

Local OPP officers were contacted and, after confirming that Brohman was trespassing, Hovingh arrived to ensure he would leave the property. Brohman was initially given a day to vacate, until the officers became suspicious of items around the trailer, seeing 20 propane cylinders and a "clearing that was being used to grow marijuana plants," the report states, worth an estimated $100,000.

The officers decided to arrest Brohman and asked him to step outside. When he refused to come out of his trailer and locked the door, Hovingh took a shovel from Brohman's truck to pry open the door before using an axe to force the door open.
Hovingh's partner, another OPP officer, shouted at Brohman to show his hands and exit the trailer but he refused, the SIU said, at one point saying: "Go away. I'm not going through this again."
At this point, Hovingh stepped inside the trailer and took a few steps forward. Brohman then moved toward his bedroom before turning around holding a shotgun, the SIU report said.
Brohman fired three shots and Hovingh "quickly returned fire, discharging seven rapid rounds from his 9mm semi-automatic pistol," the report states.
Hovingh's partner and two civilian witnesses retreated from the trailer and took cover, the OPP officer reporting that help was needed immediately.

"Shots fired, shots fired, I need assistance now!" the officer said over the police radio at 11:01 a.m., telling the dispatcher that Hovingh was inside the trailer and he didn't know the status of other man, now known to be Brohman.

"We went in to help this guy out and he pulled a gun from around the corner. Hovingh and the accused were both in the, were all in the trailer," the officer later said, according to a summary of the radio calls contained in the report.

Officers began arriving, first from the Anishnaabe police service, and helped contain the scene while waiting for the OPP's Emergency Response Team (ERT), who arrived at 12:30 p.m. After they entered the trailer, paramedics began giving first aid to Hovingh, who was breathing but unconscious.

Hovingh and Brohman were taken to hospital, where they were pronounced dead. Hovingh was shot twice in the leg; an autopsy concluded Hovingh died of shotgun wounds to his left thigh. Brohman died of gunshot wounds to the head and chest.

In his decision, Martino notes that not only was Hovingh justified in shooting in self-defence, but it was also "a reasonable response" in defence of the lives and safety of his partner and the two civilian witnesses, who were all in the vicinity of the trailer at the time of the shooting.

"Faced with an armed individual shooting at him, Cst. Hovingh could only have concluded that all of their lives were in imminent peril if Mr. Brohman was left unchecked and allowed to exit the trailer," Martino wrote.
"It is entirely conceivable that Cst. Hovingh's actions served to deter what could well have been a continuing risk to the lives and limbs of others around him."

Martino also commented on the 90-minute gap between the shooting and the entry into the trailer by paramedics and OPP's ERT, noting he was "unable to fault" other officers on scene for waiting for the specialized police to arrive before entering the trailer. Although they knew Hovingh was injured, no one knew the status of Brohman.
"As far as they knew, he could easily have been lying in wait in the trailer still capable of inflicting grievous bodily harm or death," the report states.

Martino noted investigators found firearms in the trailer and "dozens" of incendiary materials on the property, and that a civilian witness, after hearing about the shooting, called police to warn them that the property "might be booby-trapped with pipe bombs and propane tank bombs."
"In the circumstances, I am satisfied that the decision to wait to deploy an ERT team - with their specialized training and resources - was an entirely prudent one," Martino wrote.
Hovingh, 52, was a husband and father of four. At his funeral, OPP Commissioner Thomas Carrique said the death left him and the force with a "broken heart."
